This is probably a semnet issue.
     Your modification indices are keyed to the robust fit results that you have obtained, not the plain ML results. Researchers most commonly see that robust estimation makes a better looking chi-square and a more favorable fit picture, but not always. Excess kurtosis (a leptokurtic distribution) inflates the ML chi-square and worsens apparent fit. So applying the robust adjustment makes the fit seem better.
     On the other hand, a platykurtic distribution (flatter, with less kurtosis, than we would expect in a multi-normal distribution) reduces the chi-square and improve the apparent fit. So, if you apply the robust correction, the fit seems to get worse. That is probably what is happening in this case. You can check whether your data are platykurtic using the mardia function in the psych package.

On 7 June 2016 at 00:59, Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> wrote:

This is probably a semnet issue.
     Your modification indices are keyed to the robust fit results that you have obtained, not the plain ML results. Researchers most commonly see that robust estimation makes a better looking chi-square and a more favorable fit picture, but not always. Excess kurtosis (a leptokurtic distribution) inflates the ML chi-square and worsens apparent fit. So applying the robust adjustment makes the fit seem better.
     On the other hand, a platykurtic distribution (flatter, with less kurtosis, than we would expect in a multi-normal distribution) reduces the chi-square and improve the apparent fit. So, if you apply the robust correction, the fit seems to get worse. That is probably what is happening in this case. You can check whether your data are platykurtic using the mardia function in the psych package.
